title: No compulsion
hookLine: there is no compulsion in religion; the right way is distinct from error (2:256)

lines: YOU CAN MAKE SOMEONE SAY THE WORDS.
YOU CAN'T MAKE THEM MEAN IT.
cards: You can make someone sit through a sermon. You can make them memorize a creed, stand in a row, say the words.
What you can't do is make them mean it; ask any parent who has tried to make a teenager love a book, a sport, or a grandmother's favorite song.
Right after the Throne verse, the one about who holds the heavens and the earth, al-Baqarah says something about forcing. Today: no compulsion.

teach.h: THE RIGHT WAY IS DISTINCT FROM ERROR
teach.b: Verse two hundred fifty-six, in Pickthall's words: “There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error.” The second sentence explains the first.

The Arabic words are rushd, right guidance, maturity, and ghayy, straying. Some commentators read the link this way: the truth has been made clear, as clear as the verse before it, so there's no need to force anyone.
A person sees, or doesn't, and chooses. Abu Dawud preserves a report from Ibn Abbas about why the verse came down.
Some women of Medina, before Islam, had vowed that if a child of theirs survived, they'd raise it among a Jewish tribe.
Years later, when that tribe was leaving Medina, some of those children, now grown and Jewish, were among them.

teach.h: LET THEM GO AS THEY ARE
teach.b: Their Muslim parents wanted to hold them back and make them Muslim. The verse answered: no compulsion. Let them go as they are.
The verse ends with a picture: whoever turns from taghut, the Qur'an's word for whatever is wrongly worshipped, and believes in God, has grasped the firmest handhold, which will never break.
A handhold is something you grab yourself; nobody can grab it for you.
Scholars have discussed how far the verse reaches: some early jurists limited it, while others read it as a broad principle that belief can't be forced.
Look back at the week: the fast that holds back, nearness in the middle of it, clean hands, a journey without quarrels, plain answers, the one who never tires. Each one chosen, not forced.

how: Muslims widely cite 2:256 as a foundational principle that faith cannot be forced; classical and modern scholars have discussed its scope, and many read it as a general rule for how Muslims relate to people of other beliefs.

o: belief can't be forced; the right way is made clear
people may not discuss their faith with others
no religious duty is required of anyone at all

p: parents told to let their children go
grasped yourself; it will never break

s: 2:256 comes right after the Throne verse
the clear picture of God in 2:255 is followed by: no compulsion.
in Ibn Abbas's report, the parents were told to keep their grown children by force
the verse answered them: no compulsion. let them go as they are.
every scholar has read the verse in exactly the same way
some early jurists limited it; others read it as a broad principle.

games.q: your grown child, raised in another faith, is leaving with that community. you want to hold them back and make them Muslim. what does the verse say?
o: hold them back; it's for their good.
no compulsion in religion; let them go.
games.why: no compulsion. in Ibn Abbas's report, this is the moment the verse answered: let them go as they are.

practice: Picture someone who sees something important differently from you, faith, politics, how to raise children, saying what they believe in their own words.
Notice the urge to correct, convince or win, and then picture letting them be, still wishing them well.

wordCard.voice: No compulsion. Al-Baqarah 2:256: there is no compulsion in religion; the right way has been made distinct from error. Belief is a handhold you grasp yourself. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: there is no compulsion in religion (2:256); ikrah means forcing someone against their will.

carryVoice: Your line: a handhold you grasp yourself. It has to be your own hand. That's the week.
